headline: Sea Bright Rocks at Dawn: Snappers and Cocktail Blues Carry the Session, Bass a No-Show
subhead: Porgies fill the gap on the reefs while bass sit out the heat, and the first rainfish push has the northern inlets on albie watch.
body_markdown:
First light on the Sea Bright rocks this week looked about how it's looked for two weeks straight — a handful of regulars working the north jetty with swimmers and darters, getting nothing but the occasional swirl and a lot of quiet water. Down at Manasquan Inlet the jetty crews were doing the same dance, tossing pencil poppers into the current seam off the north wall on the last of the ebb and coming up with blues instead of bass. That's the story right now up and down this stretch — bass fishing is sitting in the same summer holding pattern it's been stuck in since the middle of the month, and nobody working the rocks is going to tell you different.

We flagged this last week — said stripers would stay sparse until a real cool-down kicks the fall push into gear, and that's exactly what the rocks are showing. Water's still warm enough that the bass that are around are doing their business after dark or tucked into deeper holes, not chasing bait in the wash at sunrise. Until nighttime temps start sliding — and there's no sign of that happening in the next 72 hours with high pressure holding and southwest wind sitting in that 8-to-12-knot range — this pattern isn't breaking. The fish will show. Just not yet.

What's filling the gap, and filling it well, are porgies. The nearshore reefs off Shark River and Belmar have been stacking up with them, and boats working bottom rigs with clam and squid strips in 30 to 45 feet are having no trouble putting a mess in the cooler. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and with bass this quiet it's the best bet going right now if you want bent rods without waiting until midnight. Bring light tackle — these aren't the jumbo porgies of October yet, but there are enough keeper-sized fish mixed in to make the trip worthwhile.

Bluefish remain the backbone of this whole zone and that hasn't changed. Snapper blues are thick in Shark River and the Manasquan back bay, small enough that a kid with a bare gold hook and a piece of bunker will load up in twenty minutes off the Belmar bridge or the docks along the Shark River channel. The bigger cocktail blues, two to four pounds, are mixing into the surf catch on metal — Ava 27s and 17s worked with a jigging retrieve off the Sea Bright rocks and the Asbury Park jetties on the incoming tide have been the go-to. Trollers working bunker spoons off Long Branch and Sea Bright are also connecting with better cocktail-class fish, particularly in that 20-to-40-foot band just outside the surf line.

Fluke are the soft spot this week, and there's no sugarcoating it. The warm surface layer has spread these fish out across the flats instead of concentrating them, and catch rates everywhere except the deeper structure have gone flat. The exception is the channel edges — Manasquan Inlet's deeper cuts near the Coast Guard station, and the Shark River Inlet channel itself, are still holding fish tight to the bottom where a cooler layer persists. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges on the last two hours of the outgoing, are still producing keepers in the 18-to-22-inch range, but you're working for every fish. Don't expect the easy fluke bite of June — this is a grind pattern now, best worked with the tide doing the work for you rather than burning gas running spot to spot.

Bunker are still thick along this beachfront, rolling in tight pods off Belmar and Spring Lake, and every guy on the rocks with eyes has noticed it. The ingredients for a real blitz are sitting right there — bait pinned against the beach on a falling tide, blues already working it hard from underneath. What's missing is the bass showing up to finish the job, and until that water cools a notch, the blitzes we're seeing are blue-only affairs. Worth watching daily, because when the bass do slide in on top of that bait, it won't take much warning.

The other thing worth keeping an eye on: rainfish are starting to show tighter along the beachfront as the canyon action to the south pushes bait north, and that's exactly the setup that precedes the first false albacore and bonito showings at the northern inlets. Manasquan's inlet tip and the Shark River jetties are historically the first spots in this zone to get a look at albies once that bait shows in earnest — nothing confirmed yet, but the ingredients are lining up earlier than usual this year.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full over the next few days, which means bigger tidal swings and sharper current at the inlets — good news for anyone working the fluke edges or hoping to be in position when the first albie run finally announces itself. If you've only got one morning to give it this week, split time between the porgy reefs at first light and a couple hours working metal on the Sea Bright or Manasquan rocks behind it. The bass will be back. Right now, the rocks are just asking for patience.
